en: First Chapter. At the beginning of the work, desiring the unimpeded completion of what he has intended to undertake, [the author] brings about the presence of the Goddess of Speech, as she is the presiding deity of all verbal compositions— Vijñapriyā:
I meditate upon Ananta as he seeks to appease his beloved wife, who, seeing her own reflection in the Kaustubha gem, had become offended by the thought that it was another woman held in his heart.

Having repeatedly examined the treatises on poetics (*alaṅkāraśāstra*) beginning with the *Bhūṣaṇa* and others, as well as the entirety of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* along with its root-commentaries, Bhaṭṭācārya Maheśvara composes this commentary, *Vijñāpriyā*, which clarifies the *Sāhityadarpaṇa*—the pinnacle of literary science—and delights the virtuous. (2)

With the verse beginning "śaradindu... and so forth, the author introduces his own verse at the commencement of the work—meaning at the beginning of this very work titled *Sāhityadarpaṇa*. "At the commencement" (*ārambhe*) refers to the time of the beginning of the work.
The meaning is that [the author] brings about and produces favorability and propitiousness toward the Goddess of Speech (Vāgdevatā).
In this context, the author of the work himself should be understood as the agent.
Because the time of commencement is broad and by virtue of suitability, it should be understood that the bringing about of propitiousness occurs precisely at the time preceding that.
Nor should it be asked how this was stated, given the absence of any word in the verse that indicates the act of establishing presence;

for this is obtained through the praise in the form of describing his beauty in the verse beginning with "śaradindu" (the autumnal moon), as well as through the prayer for illumination in order to destroy the darkness within one's own mind.

This is because there is an invariable rule that what is praised becomes favorable, and because the prayer is directed specifically toward obtaining that favor. Furthermore, even though the meaning has been illuminated in the mind, it is feared that the completion of the work might not occur due to obstacles.
Since the completion of the work without obstacles is also desirable due to the presence of that [deity], he says "without obstacles.

Even though mere completion depends upon worldly causes, the destruction of those obstacles occurs precisely through the favor of the deity; thus, by the desire for a completion characterized by the absence of obstacles, the qualifying element consisting of the absence of obstacles is also made an object of that desire, just as the element of happiness is [the object] of the desire "May I be happy."

Regarding the fruit, which is the completion of the work he intends to begin, he states that qualification in order to demonstrate her swiftness in action compared to other deities: "vāṅmayā" (presiding over speech). Here, the suffix *mayaṭ* is used in the sense of the base word itself;
the meaning is "she for whom speech is presided over.
In reality, however, the authoritative reading is "vāṅmayādhikṛtatayā" (by virtue of being presided over by the realm of speech).
And thus it is shown that the fruit consisting of the completion of the work—which is composed of speech—without obstacles can indeed be granted quickly by the Goddess who presides over speech.
Locanā:
(lo, a) I bow to the Supreme Goddess, who arises supported at the *mūlādhāra*.
[They] describe this entire world as a manifestation. // 1 //
There was a virtuous man, the minister of the court of the lord of Trikalinga, who was like a moon to the ocean of milk that was the Kapiñjala lineage. // 2 //

Śrī Vāchanātha, the sovereign of poets, who is a serpent among those skilled in the charms of all languages without exception, a helmsman on the ocean of the science of literature, and the leader of those whose intellects are matured by the resonance of the *dhvani* theory. (3)

By him was composed a work titled *Sāhityadarpaṇa* (The Mirror of Literature), which consists of very few syllables, possesses clearly intelligible meaning, and has all defects entirely destroyed. // 4 //
For those on this earth who desire to reach the further shore of the ocean of the science of literature, this work of the great poet Viśvanātha serves as their boat.
The essence of the ornaments of poetry for recitation and dramatic performance, as approved by true poets:
what exists here may be found elsewhere, but what does not exist here is not found anywhere.

For the delight of the learned, I compose this commentary on this life-giving essence of the compositions of excellent poets, which brings about the understanding of meanings that are difficult to comprehend. (7)

Here, indeed, while clarifying the meaning of the very sūtras through a commentary (*vṛtti*), [the author] introduces at the beginning of the work a verse (*kārikā*) that indicates the propitiation of his chosen deity—attained through the tradition of unobjectionable and virtuous conduct—in order to dispel obstacles. He begins with the word "grantha":
an obstacle (*vighna*) is either the presence of evil that acts as a hindrance or the absence of merit that impels one toward the task.
The absence of that [doubt] is a *nirvingha* (unimpeded) *avyayībhāva* compound.

The collection of objects of knowledge (*prameyajāta*) intended to be undertaken— that is, desired to be commenced— consists of the defining characteristics of poetry in both its visible and audible forms.

Its completion consists in the conclusion of the intended subject matter without any faltering. By the term "consisting of speech" (*vāṅmayī*), it is intended that the Goddess is the fulfiller of the present purpose, as she is worshipped by Brahmā and other gods for her capacity to bestow the power of eloquence prescribed in her own scripture.
May that Goddess, whose luster is as beautiful as the autumnal moon, [inspire] my speech in my heart.
Having dispelled the continuous darkness, may it illuminate all objects without exception.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, kha) "Like the autumn moon," and so forth;
[he] possesses a beautiful luster like that of the autumn moon.
That renowned goddess of speech, Sarasvatī,
has dispelled the darkness— ignorance equal to actual darkness— that was continuously spread throughout my mind.
The meaning is: "having removed [all darkness], may it illuminate all the objects that I am about to describe.

Here, by the power of the *luptopamā* (elliptical simile) in the first quarter, there is the constant possession of beautiful luster even by the autumnal moon, its capacity to destroy the darkness of the substance of continuous gloom, and its illumination of all objects such as jars and cloths.
It is established;
and thus, through these points of similarity, the relationship of the standard of comparison and the object compared between the autumn moon and the goddess Gīr is to be understood.
— *Locanā*:

"Autumn," and so forth: [the phrase] "the beautiful luster of the autumn moon" is a case of *adhyavasāna* (poetic identification), where the subject is identified as the autumn moon itself because its luster is as beautiful as that of the autumn moon. "She" (*sā*) refers to her who is well-known for being the bestower of the splendor of speech and other such qualities to the four-faced one (Brahmā) and others. "Darkness" (*tamaḥ*) refers to both ignorance and physical gloom.
The "objects" (arthān) are the intended objects of knowledge, such as jars and cloths.
Since this treatise possesses fruitfulness through its status as an auxiliary to poetry by means of the very fruits of poetry, he states those fruits of poetry:
"The attainment of the fruits of the four aims of life comes easily even for those of limited intellect."
Since it arises from poetry alone, its essential nature is therefore defined by that [poetry].

The attainment of the fruits of the four aims of human life is indeed well-established through the instruction on engaging in what ought to be done and desisting from what ought not to be done, such as: "One should proceed like Rāma and others, and not like Rāvaṇa and others.
*Vijñapriyā*:
"As a constituent part of poetry" means that it is a constituent part by virtue of being the subject of poetic analysis.
The "fourfold group" (caturvarga) consists of dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa;
the meaning is the attainment of such a result.
He demonstrates that poetry brings about the attainment of the results of the fourfold group by saying: "like Rāma and others."

"By means of the instruction on engagement and withdrawal"—through the instruction on engagement, merit arises directly for one who engages; through the instruction on withdrawal, merit arises for one who withdraws both by way of the non-arising of obstructing demerit and [the resulting state].
Thus, in both ways, they (the Vedas) possess the quality of being the means of attainment.
But from the merit (*dharma*) produced by engagement, objects and so forth arise directly.
Locanā:
(lo.i) "Not even a fool engages in action without aiming at a purpose"—this is the introductory statement for the treatise on the examination of poetry (*kāvyaparīkṣā*) being composed here.

Since the purpose (*prayojana*) must be stated, and according to the maxim that "the subsidiary (*aṅga*) possesses fruit only through the fruit of the principal (*aṅgin*)," he introduces the second verse, which sets forth the fruit of poetry, with the words "of this" (*asya*).
Its status as a subsidiary to poetry is due to its being a treatise for the examination of poetry.
There are four categories: dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
By the phrase "engagement in what ought to be done and what ought not to be done," the status of poetry as a treatise (*śāstra*) is demonstrated.
As they say: "Engagement or withdrawal, whether by means of that which is eternal or that which is produced..."
That by which men are instructed is called a śāstra.

[Objection: But how can works such as the *Mālatīmādhava*, the *Ratnāvalī*, and the *Mṛcchakaṭika*—which are composed by poets based on existing narratives—possess authority regarding their own subject matter?

And since a word that is not of the nature of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) cannot be a scripture (*śāstra*), [the author] says here: “Poetry is for us the most excellent means of valid cognition, indeed a means of valid cognition in every respect, because it originates from the cognition consisting of the tasting of self-revealing aesthetic flavor (*rasa*).”
Thus [it is said].
However, riddles (*prahelikā*) are specific types of sentences characterized by a hidden meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*), or they are insipid (*nīrasa*).
For example: "Who are those devoted to nourishing their wives? What is the cool water-bearer? The Gaṅgā."
"Whom did Kṛṣṇa strike? Whom, though powerful, does the cold not afflict?"—
in this instance, the meaning in the form of a question is the expressed (vācya), while the meaning in the form of the answer is the suggested (vyaṅgya).

If it is argued that knowledge of the *vibhāva* and other factors— which are not essentially inseparable [from the emotion]— cannot produce the valid cognition (*pramiti*) of rasa, just as the cognition of smoke superimposed upon steam cannot produce the cognition of an actual fire, then he says in response to that: "Just as through the cultivation of the true nature of the self, which is distinct from the body and so forth,
there arises a clear realization of reality (*tattvasākṣātkṛti*) that is a valid cognition (*pramā*), even though it is not a valid cognition in the ultimate sense (*tattvataḥ*)."

"In the same way, even though the cognition of the excitants (*vibhāva*) and so forth does not directly delineate them [as real], there is likewise a manifestation (*vyakti*) of the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) and so forth within literary contexts and the like."
Thus, here the logical principle is that of "conjunction" (anvācaya);

for [the factors such as] context and so forth are a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) because they produce the relish of aesthetic flavor (*rasāsvāda*), or because they constitute poetry (*kāvyatva*).
Whatever is thus is so,
just as in the case of the Rāmāyaṇa and other such works; and this [work] is likewise.
Therefore, it is "so" (tathā).
That which is not thus is not so, just as in the case of a riddle (*prahelikā*).

[Objection: But even if the context and so forth possess the nature of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and form, since they do not exist after the tasting of *rati*, they lack the demonstration of benefit or harm; therefore, how can they be said to be motivated by the capacity to cause engagement in what is beneficial or withdrawal from what is harmful?
For it should not be asked how this constitutes a treatise (*śāstra*); for it is said: "The instruction [of the world] is well-known through the observation of dramas and the like;
by observing the effects, one postulates causes consistent with them"—according to this principle, truth or falsity is determined by the power of the description.
“Through that throbbing poetic composition, men acquire proficiency;
they also develop an inquiry into the truth or falsity of the sentiments and other elements within the characters’ actions.”
At the very time of learning [the word], it exists; however, that later [usage] is sufficient as a mere scare tactic for children, like saying, "There is a crow in the middle of the garden."
Even if it lacks validity regarding its own object, does it not serve as a means for linguistic proficiency?
It will be stated later that rasa is of the nature of cognition because of its identity [with it].
Furthermore, no subsequent sublation arises regarding that [cognition], as is the case with the cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl, because it is not a cognition of invalidity.
And it has been said by Bhāmaha:
"The cultivation of excellent poetry produces proficiency in virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation, as well as in the arts; it creates fame and joy."
Thus it is said.

Furthermore, O Blessed One, the attainment of dharma through poetry is well-established both through the hymns to the lotus feet of Lord Nārāyaṇa and such Vedic statements as: "A single word, well-employed and correctly understood, becomes a cow of plenty in the heavenly world."
The attainment of wealth is established by direct perception;
the attainment of sensual pleasure occurs through the gateway of wealth alone; and the attainment of liberation results from not pursuing the fruits of the dharmas produced by these [other goals].
And because it imparts proficiency in the statements conducive to liberation.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, gha) *Kalā* means cleverness or skill.
Expertise is the impelling knowledge because it provides instruction for action;

this is because there is no pursuit of a result produced by that [mere knowledge] alone. In this context, the results are the attainment of Kāśī and the practice of yoga, since [the text] brings about proficiency through the observation of Sanskrit found within the poetry, which leads to such proficiency.
And these fruits belong specifically to the various types of poetry (*kāvyaviśeṣa*).

Thus, regarding the purpose of all poetry—what was stated by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, namely, "Poetry [leads] to fame and wealth"—that has already been stated in the very passage, "It produces renown and pleasure.
It should be understood that its possession of fruit is due to that very fruit of all poetry.
Locanā:
(Lo, ī) "Well-employed" means spoken without contradicting grammar;
it refers to speech conducive to liberation, such as the Vedas and other scriptures.
In this regard, its capacity to facilitate proficiency arises from its power to convey the relationship between words and their meanings.

Indeed, the attainment of the fourfold aims of human life (*caturvarga*) results from the Vedic scriptures only with difficulty and only for those of mature intellect, owing to their lack of aesthetic flavor.
However, because it generates a multitude of supreme joys, it results from poetry alone, and even for those of tender intellect, it arises through ease.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ṅa) [Objection: Since the Vedic scriptures exist as the means for accomplishing the fruits of the four aims of human life, for what purpose would people engage in poetry? To this, he says: "The attainment of the fruits of the four aims...
Locanā:
He explains "Sukhāditya" and so forth with the words "caturvarga" etc.

"Supreme bliss" (*paramānanda*) consists of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and the like; it is a mass of such flavors in which all other objects of cognition have dissolved. This is used figuratively because [the work] generates that [bliss]. "Those of delicate intellect" (*sukumāramatayaḥ*) refers to those whose minds are solely inclined toward pleasure, such as princes and others.
Those whose intellects are matured and who have acquired ease through the practice of the Vedas and other sciences—

surely, one should not even ask why those of matured intellect should exert effort in poetry when the Vedic scriptures exist. For if a disease that must be cured by bitter medicine can instead be cured by white sugar, which patient would not consider the application of that sugar to be superior?
Furthermore, the worthiness of poetry is also stated in the *Agni Purāṇa*:
"Human birth is rare in this world; therein, knowledge is very rare;
poetic talent is rare therein; and therein, creative power is very rare."
Thus it is said:
"Drama is the means for accomplishing the three aims of life.
And likewise in the Viṣṇu Purāṇa:
“Whatever poetic compositions there may be, and all songs as well—
these are portions of the high-souled Viṣṇu, who bears the form of sound.”
Thus,
by that reason, the nature of that poetry is defined;
by this, its subject matter is also demonstrated.
Vijñapriyā: (vi,
ca) "And thus [it is] the subject matter" means that this is the subject matter of this treatise for the purpose of defining poetry.
Locanā: (lo,
ū) Śakti is a specific latent impression (*saṃskāra*) in the form of the seed of poetic genius, without which poetry would not flow forth, or if it were to flow forth, it would be laughable.
Drama (*nāṭya*) refers to plays (*nāṭaka*) and the like that are to be performed.

Desiring to demonstrate the examination of poetry (*kāvyaparīkṣaṇa*), [the author], showing the contradiction with the objects of knowledge (*prameya*) found in the definitions of ancient poetry, says: "What is its essential nature? He replies: "That which is free from defects... Here, "that" (*tat*) refers to poetry;
"defects" (*doṣāḥ*) refer to harshness to the ear (*śrutikaṭu*) and so forth.

The "qualities" (guṇas) are sweetness and so forth; by the phrase "sometimes even without ornaments," it is indicated that while in all cases both word and meaning constitute poetry when possessed of ornaments,
there is no loss of the status of poetry even in the occasional absence of manifest ornaments.

In response to the inquiry as to what the essential nature of poetry (kāvya) is, someone says: "It consists of word and meaning that are free from defects and possessed of qualities; furthermore, they may or may not possess ornaments. This [view] is to be examined.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, cha) "Someone" means the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*. For instance:

If it were accepted that only a work free from defects constitutes poetry, then consider this verse: “This is indeed my humiliation: that my enemies exist; and among them, this ascetic; and he, right here, is slaughtering the race of Rākṣasas! Oh, Rāvaṇa still lives!
Fie, fie upon the conqueror of Indra! What is the use of having awakened Kumbhakarṇa? Or what is the use of these arms, puffed up in vain for plundering the petty village of heaven?”
Thus [ends the section]. *Vijñapriyā*:
"This indeed is an insult"—this is the utterance of Rāvaṇa, who was overwhelmed by Śrīrāma after Laṅkā had been seized.
That I have an enemy is itself a humiliation;
for one who subsists on the food of ascetics, to have even a single ascetic as an enemy is an extreme insult.
Let alone that slayer of Khara, Dūṣaṇa, and the others on the northern shore of the ocean—he too is slaughtering the entire race of Rākṣasas right here, and not merely two or three Rākṣasas!
Oh, what a marvel: even after such humiliation, Rāvaṇa still lives!
Or let it be that this has happened solely due to the adversity of my fate;
fie, fie upon my son Meghanāda, the conqueror of Śakra!

And what was the fruit for Kumbhakarṇa—who was possessed of such awakening (prabodhavatā), meaning he was awakened (prabodhita) by one who had thus awakened him, and who was characterized by that state of being (bhāvaktantatvena)? This is the meaning.
The suffix *ktavatu* is not used here, because it does not denote the object;
likewise, what is the use of my arms?

By what kind [of people]? By those who, in plundering me, regard even heaven as a mere hamlet—a tiny village—and who are vainly swollen with pride due to plundering that [heaven], being thus fruitlessly arrogant.
—Locanā:
"Insult"—this is a statement of despondency by Rāvaṇa while being overwhelmed by Rāmabhadra.
A "mean village" is a small hamlet (*grāmaṭikā*).
"Plundering" (*viluṇṭhana*) means shaking off or stripping away.
Because this verse is marred by the defect of failing to discern what is to be predicated (*vidheya*), it would not possess the status of poetry (*kāvyatva*);
on the contrary, its status as the highest form of poetry (*uttamakāvya*) is accepted precisely because it possesses *dhvani*.

Therefore, non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) is a defect of the definition. Regarding the phrase "failure to consider the predicate" (*vidheyāvimarśa*): because the subject (*uddeśya*) is the state of having enemies, the predicate (*vidheya*), which is the act of humiliation (*nyakkāra*), is placed first [in the compound] according to the rule: "One should state the predicate without first stating that which is to be restated (*anuvādya*)."
This restriction is based on the force of experience;
[one might argue] that it would not constitute poetry—yet this is not an acceptable conclusion (iṣṭāpatti). Therefore, he says "on the contrary" (pratyuta). The phrase "is accepted" implies "by all."
Not only by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, but by all;
[it was stated] by the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* in the *Kāvyaprakāśa*.

"By the definition, 'This [poetry] is called *dhvani* by the wise when the suggested sense (*vyaṅgya*) excels the expressed sense (*vācya*),' its status as the highest form of poetry (*uttamakāvya*) is accepted because it possesses *dhvani*;

therefore, there is the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*)."—In this regard, having inferred the author's intention to be that the absence of defects in general is a constituent of the definition, this was stated;
however, his actual intention is simply the absence of any defect whatsoever that obstructs verbal comprehension (*śābdabodha*).

Otherwise, how could the verse beginning with "Having seen the daughter of Pañcāla in that state in the assembly of kings" (*tathābhūtāṃ dṛṣṭvā nṛpasadasi pāñcālatanayām*)—which was cited as an example of suggestion (*dhvani*) accompanied by intonation (*kāku*)—be cited again as an instance of the fault of "deficiency of words" (*nyūnapadatva*)?

Or how could the verse beginning with "By whom this heinous crime was committed, approved, or witnessed" (*kṛtamanumataṃ dṛṣṭaṃ vā yair idaṃ gurupātakam*)—which was cited as an example of the Furious Sentiment (*raudrarasa*)—be cited again as an instance of the fault of "repetition" (*punarukta*)?
Therefore, the demonstration of [the definition's] lack of pervasiveness (*avyāpti*) arises solely from a failure to grasp his intended meaning.
Locanā:

(lo, ṝ) *avimṛṣṭavidheyāṃśa* is a failure of consideration regarding the predicate (*vidheya*). In the phrase "by those vainly swollen," the vanity of the swelling of the arms is intended to mean that it was produced only at that very moment.

Because that which ought to be predicated has been rendered subordinate by the poet through its treatment as a *tatpuruṣa* compound, it is perceived as something already established; thus, there is a failure to perceive the predicate as primary, which constitutes its non-specification (*anirdeśa*).
The ellipsis to be supplied is that this verse has been accepted by the former teachers (*pūrvācāryaiḥ*).
For here, the nature of *dhvani* (suggestive power) is indeed manifest in every single word.
To illustrate: in the phrase "this very one" (*ayam eva*), there is the particle *eva*, which indicates the exclusion of connection with anything else (*anyayogavyavaccheda*).
Of the word *me* as a vocative particle (*kākupada*),
of the plural form *arayaḥ*,
and of the pronoun *atraiva*.
In the phrase "nihanti jīvati," there is the verbal suffix (*tiṅ*); in "aho," there is the indeclinable (*avyaya*);
and in "rāvaṇa," there is that word whose expressed meaning has shifted to another specific sense (*viśeṣārthāntarasaṃkramitavācya*).
From the reduplication in *dhig dhig*,
from the *kvi* suffix prescribed in the sense of habitual action (*tācchīlya*) in *śakajita*,
and from the diminutive *kan* suffix in *grāmaṭikā*.

Because the prefixes *vi-* and *upa-* in *viṭhṭhuṇaṭhana* and the plural number in *bhujaiḥ* serve as specific indicators of that [suggestion], there is here a suggestion (*dhvani*) of imperceptible process (*asaṃlakṣyakrama*), namely the transitory emotion (*saṃcāribhāva*) called despondency (*nirveda*) arising from the speaker's own face.
Therefore, [the definition] suffers from the fault of under-extension (*avyāpti*).

Since the author of the *Dhvanyāloka* and others accept that "suggestion" (*dhvani*) constitutes the status of the highest poetry (*uttamakāvya*), the definition [of poetry as "that which is devoid of defects"] would fail to apply to such works in the immediately following verse.
If it is argued, "Only a certain portion here is defective, not the whole," then that portion in which the defect resides would be the cause for its being non-poetry.

Since that which possesses *dhvani* is the determinant of the status of supreme poetry (*uttamakāvya*), this work—being pulled from both sides by these two factors—would be neither poetry nor non-poetry.
Furthermore, defects such as those offensive to the ear (*śrutiduṣṭa*) and so forth do not corrupt only some portion of the poetry;
rather, they corrupt the poetry in its entirety.
For instance,
if they do not detract from the rasa— which is the very soul of poetry— their status as defects is not even admitted;
otherwise, the distinction between permanent (nitya) and non-permanent (anitya) defects would not be possible.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ña) He raises a doubt regarding the fault of [the argument] being self-refuted by his own established tenet, saying "But surely... He refutes that, saying "If so, then..."

Now, one might object that since a defect residing in a specific part does not corrupt the other parts, there would be the status of poetry (*kāvyatva*) in those parts, while there would be the status of non-poetry (*akāvyatva*) in the defective part; therefore, he says "not so" (*na ca*).
What then? It is the whole alone [that is affected].
He provides the reasoning for why it is only the whole that is corrupted: "For instance—otherwise," and so on.
The meaning is: "even when there is no defect in the *rasa* (aesthetic flavor) and so forth, which constitute the soul of poetry.
Regarding the terms "permanent defects" (*nityadoṣa*) and "non-permanent defects" (*anityadoṣa*):
defects such as *cyutasaṃskāra* (grammatical corruption) and the like are "permanent," because they detract from all *rasas*.

The meaning is that, according to that view, there would also be no established rule formulated by the learned scholars regarding the "corruption of the ear" (*śrutiduṣṭatva*) being non-permanent because it detracts from only a few sentiments such as the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*), since in their opinion the very quality of detracting from a sentiment is what constitutes a defect (*doṣa*).
*Locanā*.
A certain portion [of it],
namely the sense that they are "vainly swollen"—
this is the verse.
One might object: "Surely the conjunction of contradictory properties would apply to a single locus;

however, in this case there is no contradiction between the two, because the defectiveness of a particular element belongs to that which is a flaw, while the excellence of the same element belongs to that which is a *dhvani*. Anticipating this objection, he says: "And not... (na ca).
To the question, "How can a defect that resides merely in a subordinate element (aṅga) cause the deterioration of the poem? he says: "For instance" (*tathā hi*).
Since only those things which detract from the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) are considered defects, he asks "How so? and answers: "Otherwise" (*anyathā*).
Even though they do not constitute a fault when they detract from a rasa, there are eternal faults such as *cyutasaṃskṛti* (grammatical corruption) and others,
because these detract from all rasas.

The defects of impermanence, such as harshness of sound (*śrutikaṭu*) and the like, may in certain cases become merits; for instance, harshness of sound that has become firmly established within a *raudra* (fierce) or similar rasa functions as a merit, as seen in my father’s *Vijayanarasimha*: “Beholding the great world—half-lion and half-man—the people, unable to distinguish between the small and the large, fled for refuge to the ocean or the ocean [of the sky]. They mistook the mass of meteors formed by the clusters of sparks of light produced from his bared fangs—which were rubbed against the mountain-like necks shaken by the spreading winds of his sighs—for a multitude of falling stars.”

As stated by Dhvanikāra: "The defects such as those offensive to the ear, and whatever others have been shown to be non-constant, are declared to be avoidable only in the erotic sentiment (śṛṅgāra) which is the soul of dhvani."
Thus it is said.
Furthermore, in this way, poetry would have either very few subjects or no subject at all, because a work that is entirely free from defects is in every respect impossible.
Vijñapriyā:
"In the very essence of *dhvani*" means in the *śṛṅgāra* (erotic sentiment), which constitutes the soul of *dhvani*-poetry.
And here, the word *śṛṅgāra* is indicative of all *rasas* that possess sweetness (*mādhurya*).
Therefore, the meaning is that *karuṇa* (the pathetic) and *śānta* (the peaceful) sentiments should be abandoned by you.

Now, one might object: "Is it not the case that the very cause for [a sentiment being] eternal or non-eternal is what determines whether it diminishes or does not diminish the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)?
Furthermore, the cause for something being a defect (*doṣa*) is not the diminution of *rasa*."
However, since it is the very nature of that which has been stated as the cause [of the effect], he says "moreover" (*kiṃca*).
Locanā:
(lo, e) "In the essence of *dhvani*" means in the nature of *dhvani*.

Now, one might object: "Even for those works accepted as *uttama-kāvya* (supreme poetry), if they possess defects, let them not be considered *kāvya* at all. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Furthermore" (*kiñca*). This refers to the case where the words "faultless" (*adoṣa*) apply to both word and meaning within a single sentence. If it is argued that the negative particle (*nañ*) is used here in the sense of "slight" (*īṣad*), then by saying "poetry consists of words and meanings that have slight defects," it would follow that faultless words and meanings could not be considered *kāvya*.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṭha) Regarding the phrase "the negative particle [nañ] has the sense of 'slight'": the meaning is that the two are "faultless" because of the negative particle.
The meaning of "of the two faultless ones" is "of the word and its meaning."
The sense is that, since the absence of the status of poetry (*kāvyatva*) is accepted in the case of those [works] possessing *prauḍha* and *doṣa*,
non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) in examples such as "nyakkāra" and so forth is not a fault.
The sense is that those two, being possessed of *prauḍha* and *doṣa*, lack the status of poetry.
It should be noted that it has been stated that there is some fault because the definition consists in the absence of specific defects;
[this refers to] the negative particle (*nañ*) situated in the phrase "absence of defects" (*adoṣau*). *Locanā*: (Lo, Ai).
If two [works] were ever and in some respect created by a poet as being devoid of defects, they would not possess the nature of poetry (*kāvyatva*),
because the definition of poetry as "having slight defects" would be impossible there.
If it is argued that the definition applies provided such slightness of defect exists:
This too should not be stated as a definition of poetry, just as the definition of a gem does not include the exclusion of insect-borings and the like.
For insect-borings and such defects are not capable of subverting the "gem-ness" of a gem; rather, they only serve to establish a gradation in its desirability.
In the same way, defects such as *śrutiduṣṭa* (offensive to the ear) and others also belong to poetry.
And it has been said:
"The status of being poetry [is maintained] through its commonality with things like gems pierced by insects."
"Even when [the characters] are wicked, it is held that where the underlying sentiment (rasa) and so forth are clearly present."
Thus [ends the citation].
*Vijñapriyā* (vi, ḍa):
"When possible" means that when there is the possibility of even a slight fault in what is otherwise free from manifest defects.

And it has been said: "Where there is a clear presence (*anugama*) of rasa and the other elements whose sequence is imperceptible (*asaṃlakṣyakrama*), there poetic quality (*kāvyatā*) is recognized even in cases of defects, by way of analogy with gems and the like pierced by insects.
*Locanā*:

Regarding the phrase "pierced by insects"—the connection is that poetic quality is recognized even in defective works by way of "analogy" (*sādhāraṇyena*), which means by way of a general principle (*sāmānyena*).
Furthermore, the qualification "possessing qualities" (*saguṇatva*) is appropriate for both word and meaning;

for he himself has established that qualities are the sole attributes of *rasa* in such passages as: "Those which are the attributes of *rasa*, the principal entity, are like bravery and other traits of the self."
If it is argued that this is established through metaphorical usage because [the word] manifests the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*),
even so, it is incorrect.
*Vijñapriyā*:
(vi, ḍha) Having thus refuted the qualification "faultless," he says "furthermore" (*kiñca*) in order to refute the qualification "endowed with excellences" (*saguṇau*).

The meaning is that the metaphorical attribution of excellence (*guṇavattva*) to word and sense occurs through an indirect relationship (*paramparāsambandha*), namely, their being the manifesters of the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) which is the substratum of excellence.
Nevertheless, the qualification "endowed with excellences" has been stated [in the definition]. This is the meaning.
Locanā:
(lo, au) Having thus refuted the status of "freedom from defects" (*adoṣatva*) as a defining characteristic of poetry (*kāvyalakṣaṇa*), he now refutes "possession of qualities" (*saguṇatva*) as well.
"Unreasonable" (*anupapanna*) means that it is impossible (*asambhavī*).
"Of having rasa as its sole property" means of having rasa as its essential characteristic;
"by that very same person" refers to the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* himself; "by way of manifesting rasa" [is the reason].
The meaning is this: indeed, according to the method stated by the ancients, word and meaning are manifested as the revealers (*vyañjaka*) of rasa, and this is also accepted [by you];

therefore, qualities such as sweetness (*mādhurya*), which take the form of the suggested (*vyaṅgya*)—namely, *rasa* and so forth—are metaphorically designated as properties of the words and meanings that act as their revealers.
As he himself has said: "Furthermore, it is held that their existence in words and meanings occurs through figurative function (*guṇavṛtti*)."
He says "not so" with the words "nevertheless" (tathāpi).
The meaning is that although it is said, by way of metaphorical designation (upacāra), that poetry consists of word and meaning possessing qualities (saguṇa);
for instance:
Does rasa exist in those two— word and meaning— which are intended as the very nature of poetry, or not?
If it does not exist, then they also lack the possession of poetic excellences (guṇas), because the excellences follow the presence and absence of that [rasa].
If it exists, why was the qualifier "possessing aesthetic flavor" (*rasavantau*) not stated?
Locanā:
To [the question] "Why is it improper?", he says: "For instance... (*tathā hi*).
Regarding those two [poetry and drama], it is by way of metaphorical designation (*upacāra*).

The meaning is this: whether or not there is *rasa* in that which possesses qualities (*saguṇa*) depends entirely on the existence or non-existence of *rasa*; for it is only when *rasa* exists that something constitutes poetry (*kāvyatva*), and not otherwise.
First, he refutes the second [position] by its insignificance, saying "If it does not exist.
The meaning is that "following upon that" (tadanvaya) refers to having common properties.
He then refutes the first position—that "the essence exists"—saying "If it exists."
How so? This is the intended meaning:

if it is held that the definition of poetry applies only when both word and meaning—which manifest the poetic qualities (guṇas)—are present, then the definition suffers from the defect of being incomplete (nyūnapadatva).
If it is argued that this [completeness] is obtained through the necessity of the presence of qualities (guṇavattva) otherwise being unaccountable?
In that case, it would be more appropriate to say "endowed with moisture" (sarasau) rather than "possessing qualities" (saguṇau);
for no one ever says that "countries possess living beings."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṇa) In this context, "if" (*cet*) means "even if that were so" (*tathāpi*).
[The phrase] "for they do not possess life-breaths" (*na hi prāṇimantaḥ*) [is used].
The meaning is that no one says, "These countries possess bravery and so forth," with reference to the countries as the substrata of the living beings who are the substrata of bravery and the like.
Furthermore, this was stated by the author of the treatise due to a failure to perceive the seed of superimposition (*āropa*);
for indeed, superimposition does not occur unless the intermediate relatum, which constitutes the link in the chain [of transmission], is perceptible by the external senses.
However, where the middle constituent of a causal chain of connection is not perceptible by the external senses, such a superimposition (āropa) is indeed observed.

For example, in the cases "the wind is cold," "the water is warm," and "the wind is fragrant," such a superimposition occurs because the middle constituents of the respective chains of connection— the particles of water, fire, and flowers— are imperceptible due to their subtlety.

In the present case as well, since taste and other qualities— which are not perceived by the external senses— serve as the mediators of the indirect relationship, the superimposition of "possessing qualities" upon both word and meaning is indeed possible.
For this very reason, there is no such superimposition in the case of the statement "ether possesses sound-intensity," because in that instance,
sound— the mediator of the indirect relationship— is itself perceptible by the external senses.
Nor should it be argued that such a superimposition as "the self possesses knowledge" would result [from this],
because in that case, knowledge— which stands in a mediated relation with the pot— is not perceptible by the external senses;
for if such a superimposition does not occur, one must simply postulate the absence of other necessary causes for it.
Therefore, the teacher Udayana stated:
"When there is a superimposition (āropa), one seeks a cause; it is not the case that a superimposition occurs simply because a cause exists.

As for the superimposition "the crystal is red" despite the fact that the hibiscus flower is perceived by the external senses, in that case the hibiscus flower is not a constituent of such a causal chain, because the hibiscus flower does not reside in the crystal.

However, it should be noted by the wise that for the hibiscus flower (*japākusuma*), its proximity to a transparent substance alone is the cause of the superimposition, even when that [transparency] is absent; this is distinct [from the case of the moon].
Locanā:

(Lo, Ā)—Regarding the phrase "possessing qualities" (*guṇavattve*): the meaning is that the aesthetic flavor (*sarasatva*) of both word and sense has already been expressed by the very term *saguṇau* ("possessing qualities").

To explain this: if it is argued that the term "possessing qualities" (*saguṇau*) was stated in order to demonstrate their aesthetic essence (*sārasatva*), then by that very statement—namely, that "ornaments (*alaṅkāra*) are like bracelets, earrings, and so forth"—the definition is refuted, because an ornament merely bestows excellence (*utkarṣa*).
Furthermore, in this context, even the inclusion of the words "word and meaning" (*śabdārthau*) in the definition "those two [which are] faultless" (*tad-adoṣau*) is incorrect.
For instance, does the universal property of being poetry (kāvyatva) reside distributively across both word and meaning, like their conjunction and so forth;
or does it reside as a complete whole in each individually, like cowness and the like?
Not the first, because [the term *kāvya*] is a general category (*sāmānya*) itself.
Not the second, because it would follow that both the word and the meaning individually would possess the status of poetry (*kāvyatva*).
Although this was written by the author of this very work in his own commentary on the *Kāvyaprakāśa*, it has been omitted here out of deference to the ancients.

However, if freedom from defects and so forth were taken as the defining characteristics of poetry (*kāvyalakṣaṇa*), it would entail the consequence of contradicting the very subject matter (*prameya*) to be defined; thus, that [position] has been refuted.
If it is argued that the statement "word and meaning are possessed of qualities" intends to mean that word and meaning which manifest the qualities (guṇas) are to be employed in poetry—
no; for the possession of words and meanings that manifest qualities merely bestows excellence upon poetry, but does not constitute its essential nature.
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, ta) Now, [the author] raises the objection that the qualification "possessing qualities" (*saguṇatva*) does not constitute a part of the definition, but rather serves the purpose of instructing the poet; he refutes this with "if you say 'no'": *na cet*.

In the phrase "of the possession of word and meaning as well," the state of possessing those [word and meaning] through identity (tādātmya) is to be understood as belonging to poetry, which consists of word and meaning;
however, it does not mean the conferring of an essential nature (svarūpa), for "essential nature" is the definition (lakṣaṇa).
Nor is this objection improper, because the conferring of an essential nature is not the subject of the aforementioned doubt.
However, it must be said that [the objection] is raised precisely because [the definition] is intended to be focused on the instruction of poetry (*kāvyopadeśa*),
and not because it is improper to include the phrase "bestowing its own nature" (*svarūpādhāyakatva*) within the definition of *svarūpa*.
The meaning is, in effect, that it is inappropriate to provide the qualification "focused on the instruction of poetry" as part of the definition.
For it has been said:
"The word and the meaning constitute the body of poetry, while rasa and the like constitute its soul."
Qualities (guṇas) are like bravery and so forth;
defects (doṣas) are like being one-eyed and so forth; and styles (rītis) are like specific configurations of the limbs.
"Ornaments are like bracelets, earrings, and so forth.
By this, that which was stated— "but [the figure] is sometimes without ornament"— is also refuted.
The meaning of this is as follows: poetry consists of word and meaning which, in all cases, possess figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*), though in some instances they may even lack manifest figures.
This is because, within poetry, even when word and meaning possess figures, those figures contribute to its excellence.
By this, the statement of the author of the *Vakroktijīvita*—that "oblique expression (*vakrokti*) is the life-breath of poetry"—is also refuted.
Because *vakrokti* (indirect expression) is of the nature of an ornament (*alaṅkāra*).
In the phrase "like heroism and so forth," the ellipsis is to be supplied as "they are those which bestow excellence upon the aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)."
"Like bracelets, earrings, and so forth"— the remainder of the sense is that these are "ornaments for the word and its meaning.
"By this" means by the fact that a qualifying attribute which bestows excellence is not to be included in the definition [of a poetic figure].
"Of the word and meaning together with their ornaments"—the ultimate meaning is "of the state of the word and meaning being possessed of ornaments.
Locanā:
(i) By this, it is stated that ornaments and so forth share the same nature as bracelets, earrings, and other such [physical] ornaments.
The author of the *Vakrokti-jīvita* says: [It is so] because it consists of figurative expression (*alaṅkāra*).
For it has been stated: "This very *vakrokti* (oblique speech) exists everywhere; by means of it, the meaning is brought to light."
"The poet must exert effort in this [poetry]; what ornament can exist without it?
And as for that which was cited in some cases where the ornament is not manifest:
"He who stole my youth is indeed the same bridegroom; those same nights of Caitra; and those same mature breezes from the Kadamba trees, fragrant with blooming Mālatī flowers."
And yet, though I am that very same person, my heart yearns for that place on the bank of the Revā, at the foot of a cane tree, during the playful performance of amorous dalliance.
Thus [it is said].
This is to be considered.
*Vijñapriyā*:
The author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* cited the verse beginning with “*yaḥ kaumāraharaḥ*” (*He who took away my youth*) as an example where the poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*) is not manifest; to this,
[the commentator] says “*yac ca*,” asserting that in that case, there is indeed a manifest poetic figure.
"O you who stole my youth"—

this is the internal reflection of an unchaste woman who had made an appointment on the bank of the Revā at her own home. Although there is no longing within me, nevertheless, my mind [is drawn] to that place on the bank of the Revā where the appointment was made, beneath the shade of the reed trees (*vetasī*), for the sake of the ritual of play consisting of the act of sexual union.
The meaning is that she longs [for him].
He demonstrates the cause of her longing with the words beginning, “He who steals away maidenhood” (*yaṭha kaumārahara*).
“Maidenhood” (*kaumāra*) refers to the state of being a maiden—that is, the state of not being married.
By "marriage" (pariṇayana), he who is the bridegroom— that is, the husband— is meant; that very bridegroom is the "best" (vara),
meaning he is capable of providing pleasure according to one's desire.
He says, "those very same [nights]," because even the nights of the month of Caitra are no different here than they are at the place of appointment.
He says, "and those [winds]," because even the fragrant breeze is no different here.
"Kadamba winds" means the breezes from the Kadamba groves situated in the middle.
For this very reason, even though they are full-blown, they result in mildness; for although the forest breeze is full-blown, its mildness exists through its presence outside [the flowers].
As for fragrance, it depends entirely upon the *mālatī*.
Furthermore, in the month of Caitra, there is simply an absence of the *kadamba* flower.

Some, however, explain [the term] as referring to *dhūlīkadamba* flowers; in their view, it would follow that the qualification "mature" (*prauḍha*) applied to the wind would be inappropriate. Others, however, explain it thus: "The blossomed *mālatī* flowers, which are maturely fragrant and whose scents satisfy the sense of smell."
That is not so;
for in the expression "kadambānilās te ca" (and those kadamba breezes), since the word "te" (those) is absent, the recognition [of the referent] would be untenable.
Furthermore, if one were to supply the word "they" (*te*), the fault of breaking the thematic continuity (*prakramabhaṅga*) would arise,
and there is no factor to necessitate such an ellipsis;
as for the phrase "she too" (*sā ca*), I am likewise in that very same state.
The meaning is "in both cases.
Although there is no such cause for longing in this way, nevertheless, longing arises due to the distinct nature of the mind; this is the meaning.
Locanā: (Lo,

ī) Having thus refuted the definition of poetry, [the author] says "yacceti" (and that which...)— the remainder being that this was cited by the authors of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* as an example where a clear ornament (*sphuṭālaṅkāra*) is absent, yet they demonstrate a clear ornament therein.
Regarding the phrase "he who [spent] his youth": youth is fresh adolescence;
he who has passed it by through constant, unfeigned love is the one who took away his youth, the bridegroom chosen by her own will.
But Caitra is not made [to say] "It is spring" by his father and others,
because in that case there is an absence of the genus *kadamba*.
*Mālatī* is the *vāsantī* flower;
some say *kadamba* refers to the *dhūlikadamba*.

However, those who know the tradition explain that both seasons are included because there is no difference in their capacity to kindle the god of love—[the first] being spring itself and [the second] being the rainy season itself.

For here, there is the clarity of the figure of speech *saṃdehasaṅkara* (a blend of doubt), which is rooted in *vibhāvanā* (the description of an effect in the absence of its cause) and *viśeṣokti* (the description of an effect in the absence of its cause).
*Vijñapriyā*:
Regarding "vibhāvanā"—it is the description of longing even in the absence of the causes for longing.
This is because its definition is: "Vibhāvanā is said to be the production of an effect without a cause.
Likewise, although causes for longing—such as a husband and so forth—are present, there is a description of the absence of longing in the form of longing; thus, it is *viśeṣokti*.
For its definition will be stated later: "When the effect is absent despite the presence of the cause, it is *viśeṣokti*."
The meaning is: "of the confusion of the doubt based on that" (tanmūlasandehasaṅkarasya), that is, of the figure of speech consisting in the commingling of the doubt based on that.
There is no doubt regarding those two;
for since there is the possibility of their coexistence in a single place as non-contradictory elements, there is an absence of doubt.

However, because there is doubt regarding the relationship of primary and subordinate between the suggested *adbhuta-rasa* (the marvelous sentiment) and the semblance of *śṛṅgāra* (erotic sentiment), there is indeed a doubt between the *rasavat* and *preyas* figures of speech.

To explain: since wonder is aroused by the presence of the cause despite the absence of the effect, and by the absence of the effect despite the presence of the cause, it constitutes the *adbhuta-rasa* whose stable emotion (*sthāyibhāva*) is that [wonder].

Is this [adbhuta] a subordinate element of the semblance of *śṛṅgāra*—which is obtained through love and longing directed toward a secondary character—and thus a *rasavat* figure of speech? Or is it something else?
Because it will be stated that the figure of speech *rasavat* consists in [another] rasa being subordinate to a primary rasa;
or else, that very [figure] is the subordinate element of the *ābhāsa* (semblance) of the marvelous rasa (*adbhuta-rasa*),
since it will be stated that the figure *preyas* consists in an *ābhāsa* being subordinate.
This is because all theorists of poetics agree that two aesthetic sentiments (*rasa*) cannot be perceived independently without being in a relationship of primary and subordinate (*aṅga-aṅgin*).
Furthermore, this objection regarding "clarity" (*sphuṭatva*) is not a pleasing one;
for clarity and lack of clarity consist precisely in whether something is perceived quickly or is not perceived at all.

And thus, because there is an absence of the negative particle (*nañ*) which expresses both the non-existence of the cause and the existence of the effect, that conceptualization is indistinct due to its delay; and because those two are thus indistinct, the figures of speech based upon them, as demonstrated, are all the more indistinct.
*Locanā*:
"For here," [it is said]; since the production of an effect in the absence of a cause is *vibhāvanā*, and that is indistinct here.

Indeed, the causes of longing—such as the absence of union with the beloved—are not present here, yet longing has arisen; furthermore, their absence is established by way of the presence of the beloved’s union, which is their opposite. Thus, the excitants (*vibhāvas*) are indistinct.
If, indeed, there is a description by way of the non-existence of causes such as the absence of union with a beloved, that alone constitutes its clarity.
Furthermore, the figure of speech called *viśeṣokti* consists in the non-arising of an effect despite the presence of its complete set of causes; yet even that is not clear here.

The presence of beloved ones and so forth are the causes of steadfastness (*dhṛti*). In this context, although these causes were present, steadfastness did not arise; this has been described by way of the arising of longing (*utkaṇṭhā*), which is what is meant when it is said that "steadfastness did not arise."
In that case, since the non-arising of the effect would have been stated explicitly, the *viśeṣokti* (poetic figure of specific denial) would be manifest.
Here, however, the impossibility of maintaining composure is stated by way of the arising of longing in a contrary form;
therefore, the *viśeṣokti* is not manifest.
Thus, the author of the *Kāvyaprakāśa* maintains that because the two figures—Vibhāvanā and Viśeṣokti—are not clearly manifest here, there is an absence of distinct poetic ornaments (*alaṅkāra*).
To this, he replies: "In this case," meaning that here Vibhāvanā and Viśeṣokti are not clearly manifest.

Nevertheless, since the figure of speech *saṅkara* (blending) is clearly present when there is doubt arising from the commencement of both [figures], how can it be said that there is an absence of a clear figure of speech?
Furthermore, *saṃsṛṣṭi* (commixture) and *saṅkara* are accepted as distinct figures of speech, just as worldly ornaments such as crowns and so forth are combined.
By this—
“A poet, by composing poetry that is faultless, endowed with merit, adorned with ornaments,
and permeated by aesthetic flavor (rasa), attains both fame and pleasure.”
By this [statement], the status of these and others as definitions of poetry is also refuted.
"By this" means by the refutation stated by us.
Locanā: By this— namely, by stating that "being free from defects" does not constitute the definition of poetry—
the definition stated in the *Sarasvatīkaṇṭhābharaṇa*, beginning with "free from defects," etc., [is refuted].

Furthermore, in this context, since the term "sarasau" (possessing rasa) is already stated as the primary meaning of the scripture, the subsequent statement "saguṇau" (possessing qualities) is redundant according to the manner just explained.

As for what was stated by the author of the *Dhvanyāloka*— "Suggestion (*dhvani*) is the soul of poetry"— does that *dhvani*, characterized by the nature of things (*vastu*), figures of speech (*alaṅkāra*), and aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) and so forth, constitute the soul of poetry?
Or is it merely the form consisting of rasa and so forth?
Not the first, because it would over-extend to riddles (*prahelikā*) and the like.
If the second, we say "yes."
Vijñapriyā:
"The word 'dhvani'— " means the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*),
and not the poetry of *dhvani* (*dhvanikāvya*).
Because it is impossible for a riddle (prahelikā) and the like to possess the nature of poetry;
nor should it be argued that even such works are indeed poetry, for the status of being poetry is predicated solely on the basis of the suggestible (vyaṅgya) being something to be tasted (āsvādya).
In riddles and similar compositions, however, the poet’s intention lies precisely in the fact that the suggested meaning is not understood;
it is its very unintelligibility that constitutes its charm, rather than the presence of a relishable suggested meaning.
For instance: "Embraced by a young woman around the neck and resting upon her hips, who is it that coos repeatedly even in the presence of elders?"

In this context, since the poet’s intention lies precisely in the non-comprehension of the suggested full water-jar (*pūrṇakalaśa*), it is only here—due to its strikingness—that the *prahelikā* (riddle) constitutes a poetic figure (*alaṅkāra*).

As for the difficulty of comprehension found in the case of the "obscure" (*asphuṭa*) type of subordinate suggestion, the poet does not intend that degree of difficulty; therefore, such a suggestion is not excessively difficult to grasp, and its capacity to be aesthetically relished (*āsvādyatva*) certainly remains.
In the phrase "in riddles (*prahelikā*) and so forth," the word "and so forth" includes the concealment of the agent, the object, and other such elements.
Regarding "if it is the second"—the syllable *oṃ* signifies acceptance.
I too [hold that] "poetry is a sentence whose essence is aesthetic flavor (*rasa*)."
The meaning is that this will be stated [later].
Locanā:
(lo, ṛ) Now, desiring to establish that *rasadhvani* alone constitutes poetry while refuting the status of *vastu* and *alaṅkāra* as such, he says: "As for what... and so forth.
The author of the Dhvanyāloka is the venerable teacher Ānandavardhana.
The *vastu* (subject matter) is the mere meaning;
the *alaṅkāra* (ornament) is that same [meaning] when endowed with aesthetic charm (*vicchitti*).
*Rasa* refers to the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*) and other sentiments;

by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the emotional states (*bhāva*), their semblances (*tadābhāsa*), and other varieties of the imperceptible process of suggestion (*asaṃlakṣyakramabheda*) are included.
A *prahelikā* is a specific type of sentence characterized by a suggested meaning (*vyaṅgyārtha*) or one that is devoid of rasa.
For example:
"Who are those devoted to nourishing their wives? What is the river that carries cool water? Who is Gaṅgā? Whom did Kṛṣṇa slay? And whom does the cold not afflict, even though he is powerful?"
In this instance, the meaning in the form of a question is the expressed (vācya), while the meaning in the form of an answer is the suggested (vyaṅgya).
For instance: "Who are those devoted to the nourishment of their wives? (dārāṇāṃ bhāryāṇāṃ poṣaṇe ratāḥ ke?)
Which Gaṅgā carries cool water?
Whom did Kṛṣṇa slay? What powerful thing does cold not afflict?
Thus is the question. Regarding the response: "kedārāḥ" means fields.
Now, if it is argued that *dhvani*—consisting merely of the form of rasa and so forth—is the soul (*ātman*) of poetry, [then...]
Vijñapriyā:

(vi, pha) Now, one might object: "If it is only rasa that is the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) and constitutes the soul of poetry, then how can there be the status of 'poetry' when a mere fact (*vastu*) is the suggested meaning? Thus, he raises this doubt with the words: "Now, [if it were] merely rasa and so forth...
At that time—
"My husband is submerged here; look well here for me every day. O traveler, blinded by night, do not sink into my bed!"
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ba) "The self is here"—[as in: "My mother-in-law is bathing here; I am looking around here all day long.
O traveler blind at night, do not fall upon our bed!"
This is a speech by a messenger (dūtī) herself to a traveler who has taken up residence in her own house and who describes himself as being blind at night.
"Attā" means mother-in-law; "veśī" refers to the wife.
By the mention of the mother-in-law's immersion [in water], her state of being nearly dead is indicated.
Locanā:
(lo, ṝ) *atteti*—the word *divasakam* refers to the time for action; here, by the speech of the unchaste woman (*puṃścalī*), the mere sense is intimated: "Come fearlessly to my bedchamber."
The prima facie argument is: "How can such works as these be accepted as poetry?
He states the established conclusion: "In this case too," [it is so] precisely because they possess the semblance of rasa (rasābhāsa).
However, it is not merely because the mere object (*vastumātra*) is suggested (*vyaṅgya*).
Furthermore, there is a semblance of rasa (*rasābhāsa*) here because the passion (*rati*) of an unchaste woman directed toward another's husband is revealed.
Alternatively, even in cases where humans are the subjects, the designation of "poetry" (*kāvyavyavahāra*) is accepted on the basis of the predominance of the mere object.
If it is asked, "In cases such as these, since only the literal matter (*vastumātra*) is suggested (*vyaṅgya*), how can there be the designation 'poetry' (*kāvyavyavahāra*)?", we reply:
"No; for here too, we maintain that there is simply the presence of a semblance of rasa (*rasābhāsa*). Thus says the *Vijñapriyā*.
Regarding the phrase "the suggestion of a mere fact" (*vastumātrasya vyaṅgyatva*):

the meaning is that it is the suggestion of a mere fact such as, "You will come to my bed. Regarding the term "semblance of rasa" (*rasābhāsa*): [it refers to cases where the conditions for rasa are deficient].
It is called an "appearance" (ābhāsa) because it has a mere suggester (upanāyaka) as its object.

Even when other suggested meanings are present, poetic quality (kāvyatva) exists only when there is a culmination in rasa; otherwise, if one were to accept poetic quality in the absence of such a state, there would be the fault of over-extension (ativyāpti). Thus he says: "otherwise."

Otherwise, even in the sentence "Devadatta goes to the village," there would have to be the status of poetry (*kāvyatva*) because of the comprehension of the suggested meaning (*vyaṅgya*) consisting of his servant's following him.
If you say, "Let it be so," we reply:
no, because only that which possesses aesthetic flavor (*rasavat*) is accepted as poetry.

For the purpose of poetry has been stated by the ancients as well: namely, that by means of bestowing the mass of happiness derived from the tasting of aesthetic flavor (*rasa*), it provides instruction to those to be trained—such as princes and others of tender intellect who are averse to the Vedas and technical treatises—regarding what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, through such teachings as: "One should act like Rāma and the like, and not like Rāvaṇa and the like."
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ma) He states the reason for accepting only that which possesses rasa as being poetry: "the purpose of poetry.

By showing that the primary purpose is the giving of a mouthful of food through the tasting of rasa—just as one observes [a child's] behavior toward what should and should not be done—it is stated that such a mouthful of food is indeed the principal purpose.
It has been stated that such instruction occurs only as far as possible;
and thus: "The bedchamber was empty," and so forth; and likewise, "He who took away my youth," and so on.
In such verses as these, even in the absence of such [technical] instruction, the nature of poetry (*kāvyatva*) remains unimpaired.
*Locanā*:
Regarding the phrase "of poetry"—this is the meaning:

The tasting of aesthetic flavor (*rasāsvāda*) alone is the mouth of the poetic composition; it has been said by way of this metaphor: "People consume the meaning of the sentence mixed with the sweet flavor of poetry, just as bees drink a bitter medicine after having first licked honey."
Thus it is said; and likewise, the *Āgneya Purāṇa* also states:
"Even though the primary focus is the cleverness of speech, aesthetic flavor (*rasa*) alone is the life-breath here."
The author of the *Vyaktiviveka* has also stated: "No one disagrees that the essence of poetry is its soul, which consists of rasa and so forth."
Vijñapriyā:
(lo, e) The author of the *Vyaktiviveka* is indeed the teacher Mahima.
"Attainment of self" (*ātmalābha*) means obtaining the designation of "poet" (*kavi*), which results from the attainment of that [self], namely, the attainment of the plot (*itivṛtta*).

By the word "etcetera" (ādi), it is meant that a composition of words which does not establish that rasa alone is the life-soul of poetry [is excluded]. Now, if this is so— meaning, if the sense is that only that which possesses rasa is poetry— then what of those characters such as mountains and the like who are described as being devoid of rasa?
He states the established conclusion: a great poem (mahākāvya) is a composition whose essence is rasa;
style (rīti) is the arrangement of words, and the components are the individual words.

The author of the Dhvanyāloka has also stated: "A poet does not attain his status merely by narrating events as they occurred, for that can be accomplished through historical accounts and the like," and so forth.
If it is objected that, in that case, certain flavorless verses occurring within a literary work would not possess the status of poetry,
we say no; for just as individual flavorless words within a flavorful verse are considered flavorful by virtue of the verse's flavor,
so too those [verses] are accepted as possessing flavor by virtue of the flavor of the entire work.

As for the fact that the designation "poetry" (kāvyavyavahāra) is applied even to works devoid of rasa—due to the presence of syllables that manifest the qualities (guṇas), the absence of defects, and the presence of ornaments—that is merely secondary (gauṇa), based on the similarity to the composition of poetry possessing rasa and so forth.
As for what was stated by Vāmana: "Style (rīti) is the soul of poetry."
That is not so; for *rīti* is a specific kind of composition (*saṃghaṭanā*),
and composition consists in the arrangement of constituent parts,
whereas the self (*ātman*) is distinct from that.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ya) Eloquence of speech is an ornament;
for that which possesses the designation "poetry" contains a meaning common to the suggested sense, and thus it itself possesses the designation "poetry."
*Itivṛtta* refers to the matter already described. Regarding the phrase "quality and action":
although color (*varṇa*) is the manifester of quality alone and not of action, nevertheless, in this context, the word *varṇa* should be understood as referring to color and so forth.

And as it was stated by the author of the *Dhvanyāloka*: "The meaning that is praised by connoisseurs and established as the soul of poetry is traditionally held to have two divisions: the denoted and the suggested."

Thus, in this context, the view that the nature of poetry consists in the expressed meaning (*vācyātmatva*) is discarded precisely because it contradicts the author’s own statement: "The soul of poetry is *dhvani*. — *Vijñapriyā*.

Regarding the phrase "the expressed and the implied": here, the word *vācya* (expressed) refers to that which is distinct from the meaning of the word *pratīyamāna* (implied), namely the *vyaṅgya* (suggested);
by this, the sense of *lakṣaṇā* (indication) is also included.
Regarding the phrase "by one's own words":
"sound" (dhvani) refers to the suggested meaning (vyaṅgyārtha).
The meaning is that there is a contradiction between two of one's own statements—one stating its nature as the suggested meaning and the other stating its nature as the expressed meaning (vācyārtha).
Now, what then is poetry? It is said to be "a sentence whose soul is rasa.
We shall define the nature of rasa.
Rasa alone is the soul (*ātman*) of that [poetry], for it is the sustainer of life by virtue of its essential nature;
without it, the status of that work as poetry is not admitted.

Because of the etymological derivation "that which is relished is *rasa*," even emotions (*bhāva*), their semblances (*tadābhāsa*), and so forth are included therein. Of these, *rasa* is as follows: [Example: *śṛṇu tvaṃ...* (Listen, you... [etc.]
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, la) The question beginning with "What, then, is poetry? and so forth;
the answer beginning with "It is said" and so forth.
"Because it has been established"—the meaning is: by such [expressions] as "Devadatta goes," and so forth. (Locanā)
(Locana, Ālokamālinī) Having thus demonstrated the contradiction of the previous definitions with the object of cognition (*prameya*), he introduces his own definition.
As for the phrase "What then?"—the meaning is: if these are not the definitions of *kāvyaliṅga*.

Regarding the term "consisting of rasa" (*rasātmaka*), he says "it is tasted" (*rasyate*) to show that by the word *rasa*, all [figures] whose non-difference is unperceived (*asaṃlakṣyakrama*) are included.
It is relished (*rasyate*), that is, tasted;
"taste" (*svāda*) is of the nature of the arising of self-bliss through the merging with the meaning of the poetry, as described in the aforementioned manner.
The status of being the object (*karmatva*) belongs to rasa and the other elements only figuratively (*upacārāt*).
It will be stated that [the suffix] is used in the sense of the agent of the action (*karmakartṛ*).

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), there are semblances of rasa (*rasābhāsa*) and semblances of bhāva (*bhāvābhāsa*), as well as the subsidence (*śānti*), emergence (*udaya*), conjunction (*sandhi*), and commingling (*śabalatā*) of bhāva.
Seeing that the bedchamber was empty, she rose slightly from her bed and, feigning sleep, gazed for a long time at the face of her husband who had approached quietly.
Having kissed him confidently and seeing the horripilation on his cheeks, the young woman lowered her face in shame; then, as her lover smiled, he kissed her for a long time.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, va) "The bedchamber is empty," and so forth.
This is a description of the actions of a newly married girl whose youth has just begun to blossom.
Here, the sequence of all actions—prior and posterior—is to be understood as indicated by the gerund suffix *ktvā* in the order beginning with "having looked" (*vilokya*).
Rising slightly from her bed was for the sake of quickly concealing herself upon the awakening of her beloved;
rising slowly, however, was so that no sound might be produced.

This is an adverbial phrase describing the act of kissing: "in such a way that there was a prolonged gazing at the face, due to affection for the certainty of sleep; [and] with confidence born from the certainty of sleep, resulting in a sense of relief."
"Having seen [him], she became one whose face was bowed with shame"—this is the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*), which is to be understood from the context of the face.
For at that very moment, the use of the suffix *ktvā* is justified by the fact that there is a single agent for two actions.
In all these preceding actions, the young girl (*bālā*) is the agent.

The function of the kissing that is dear to laughter is the prolongation of the kiss; this occurs because, through the heroine’s certainty of her emotional state, fear and apprehension are absent, and an abundance of passion arises.
Here, the suggested meanings are the mutual erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgāra*) of sexual union and love-play.

The sight of the empty dwelling is the excitant (uddīpanavibhāva) of the heroine's passion (rati). The actions beginning with rising from bed and ending with bowing her face are the consequents (anubhāvas) of the heroine's passion; these same actions serve as the excitants of the hero's passion.
The kissing by the beloved and his smile are the consequents (*anubhāva*) of her love;
these two alone serve as the excitants (*uddīpanavibhāva*) for the heroine's love.
When the audience recognizes both, the emergence of rasa occurs.
Locanā: (lo, o) Having observed that the chamber for dalliance— the house of pleasure— was empty, secluded, or void, she rose from her bed.

Having risen slightly from her bed and become upright, she— meaning silently and gently— the young woman gazed for a very long time at the face of her beloved who was feigning sleep; that is to say, having looked upon it for a prolonged duration and examined it thoroughly,
she kissed him confidently and without hesitation, and tasted him, her body marked by horripilation with its hair standing on end.
The connection is as follows: having seen her cheek, the heroine—her face bowed with shame and her countenance lowered by modesty—was kissed for a long time by her laughing beloved.
The heroine is *svīyā* (belonging to herself).
The hero is favorable;
here, the poetic figure (alaṅkāra) is the variety known as *narmagarbha* (the "jest within").
[The verse begins with] "śūnyabhitti" and so forth.
In this context, the word *vilokana* contains an implied causative sense (*antarbhūta-ṇij-artha*), meaning "causing to look"; thus, it signifies "looking.
Because these two actions share a single agent, the suffix *-ktvā* is used to indicate the prior occurrence [of the first action].
In this context, the hero and the heroine are the objective excitants (*ālambana-vibhāva*);
the empty dwelling, the house, and so forth are the environmental excitants (*uddīpana-vibhāva*);
and the heroines' glances at the hero and the like, as well as the hero's feigned sleep and so forth, are the consequent manifestations (*anubhāva*).

For sleep, being undertaken under a pretext, does not constitute a transitory emotion (*vyabhicārin*); furthermore, the transitory emotions do not reside in the heroine; and through the act of looking, there arises suspicion.
From rising comes agitation;
from the slowness of rising comes fear;
and from gazing for a long time arises discursive thought born of doubt as to whether [the person] is asleep or not.
By the word "confidently," joy is indicated through the knowledge of the certainty of sleep; by the kissing, longing;
and by the gazing, restlessness.
By the word "confidently" (*viśrabdham*), shame (*lajjā*) is indeed indicated;
and through the pretext of feigned sleep, there is fortitude (*dhṛti*) belonging to the hero,
as well as longing (*autsukya*) and joy (*harṣa*) due to the long-continued kissing.

And the aesthetic emotion (*rasa*) of love (*ratibhāva*), when manifested through these factors in common, assumes the form of the erotic sentiment (*śṛṅgārarasa*). In this way, the distinction between the excitants (*vibhāva*) and the other factors should be understood even in the examples to be cited hereafter; for in this case, the sentiment is called the erotic of union (*saṃbhoga-śṛṅgāra*).
An example of *bhāva* (the state of being) is found in the work of Mahāpātra Rāghavānanda Sāndhivigrahika:
“Upon the edge of whose scales the ocean rested, upon the surface of whose back the circle of the world, and upon whose tusk the earth— ”
The Lord of the sons of Diti [Rāhu] is in his nails; the two worlds [Heaven and Earth] are in his feet;
and the host of Kṣapaṇakas is in his anger.
In his arrow is the Ten-faced one (Rāvaṇa), in his hand the demon Pralamba,
and in his meditation the entire multitude of the unrighteous.
Salutation to this someone.
In this context, the emotion (*bhāva*) is the longing directed toward the Blessed One.
*Vijñapriyā* [comments]: "Of him who dissolved [into her]."
Salutation to this certain indefinable one—Nārāyaṇa, who in effect possesses ten incarnations—who has been brought near by his very feet.
He states his qualities according to the distinctions of the ten incarnations, beginning with the Fish, starting with the words "of whom":
although the Fish was small, it is described with hyperbolic language (prauḍhokti) as being so great that even the dissolution [of the world] occurred within the limit of its scales.
Regarding the word "pṛṣṭhe" (on the back): this refers to the Kūrma incarnation.
The verb "alīyata" (disappeared) is to be construed with every [instance].
Because of the vastness of his back, the entire circle of the world—that is, the circle of the earth—[rested] upon it.
"In the tusk" refers to the Varāha incarnation;
"the lord of the sons of Diti" is Hiraṇyakaśipu,
which refers to the Narasiṃha incarnation.
"Rodasī" refers to heaven and earth;
"this" refers to the Vāmana incarnation;
and "wrath" refers to the Paraśurāma incarnation.
"Dhyāna" [is so called] because in the descent as Buddha he meditates upon all things;
"asau" [is so called] because in the descent as Kalki he cuts down the Mlecchas with a sword.
Locanā:
(lo, au) Regarding the phrase "in whom he dissolved"—this refers to the description of the ten incarnations (*avatāra*) of the Blessed One.
Here, the verb "he dissolved" (*alīyata*) is to be construed with each subsequent sentence. Thus, "the ocean dissolved in the bark-garment region" (*śalkasīni valkalapradeśe*), and so forth.
By this [mantra], one becomes the Fish;
by the thought "the circle of the world dissolved into the region of my back," one becomes the Tortoise;
and in the same way, the Boar and the others.
Because it is impossible to specify it for any particular individual.
An example of a semblance of rasa (rasābhāsa) is as follows:
"The bee, following its own mate, drank honey from a single flower."
And the black antelope scratched with his horn the doe, whose eyes were closed from the sensation of touch.
Vijñapriyā:
(vi, ṣa) "The honey-bee" (*madhudvirepha*)—this is a description of the amorous behavior even of animals when an untimely spring has arisen to break the asceticism of Maheśa.

Here, the drinking of honey together with the beloved and the scratching of the beloved by the bee and the black antelope (*kṛṣṇasāra*) are the *anubhāvas* (consequent emotions) of their passion (*rati*).
The manifestation (*bhāsa*) of those two [types of] *śṛṅgāra* occurs through their horizontal extension;
"and so on for others" means that manifestations of emotions (*bhāvābhāsa*) and so forth are also like this.
And they will be shown first.
Locanā:
(lo, a) [is] in a single vessel in the form of a flower.
In this case, because the erotic sentiment of union (*sambhoga-śṛṅgāra*) has animals as its object, it is a semblance of rasa (*rasābhāsa*).
The same applies to other cases.
Furthermore, what is the nature of defects (*doṣa*) in poetry?
Vijñapriyā:
"Furthermore, the defects" means those whose presence destroys the status of being poetry (*kāvyatva*).
As for the question of what their essential nature is or in what form they exist, the explanation is as before.
Thus they are called:
defects are those which detract from it,
such as being offensive to the ear (*śrutiduṣṭa*), lack of full meaning (*apuṣṭārthatva*), and so forth, just like being one-eyed, being lame, and so on.
Whether by way of word and meaning or by way of the body [of the poem],
